label: Where machine learning helps in EDA
lesson:
# Where machine learning helps in EDA

Machine learning is one branch of EDA, not a replacement for it. Placers, routers, timers and verifiers are built on algorithms with guarantees and on physics with known error. A learned model is useful when it gives a fast, approximate answer that steers one of those engines, and harmful when it is trusted where a guarantee is needed. A tool designer's first job is to tell the two cases apart.

## Where learning pays

Learning pays when three conditions hold. The exact evaluation is expensive or not yet available: post-route wire delay is unknown at placement time, and a full global route per placement move is too slow. Many similar instances recur, so experience transfers: every block in a project runs the same flow with similar netlists. And an approximate answer is good enough because something exact runs later. Under those conditions a model can rank 200 flow configurations from early features so that only ten get full runs, or give the placer a congestion map between expensive routes. Where the exact answer is cheap (the HPWL of a net, an overlap check, a topological order), a model only adds error and runtime.

## What learning cannot replace

Some questions have answers that must hold for every input, and a model trained on samples cannot give them. Legality is one: a placement either has overlapping cells or it does not, and a legalizer enforces that exactly. Manufacturability is another: only a DRC engine running the real rule deck on the real geometry decides it. Functional equivalence of two netlists is a formal property proven by an equivalence checker. Signoff timing is a conservative bound computed by propagating worst-case delays over every path. A predictor's error is measured on a test set and has no guaranteed bound on an unseen design. So a prediction of zero DRC violations, or of positive slack, licenses nothing at signoff.

## Propose with a model, decide with an engine

The pattern that makes learning safe is simple: the model proposes and an exact engine decides. A model suggests 50 buffer insertions; incremental STA checks each one. A learned net ordering guides a router; the router still enforces design rules. In the four-layer engine model the learned part lives in the strategy layer, feeding guidance to a core that keeps invariants, so the worst a bad model can do is a legal but poor result. The other half of the decision is cost. A method that matches a heuristic's quality but needs three GPU-days of training per design is useful only if that cost is amortized across many designs.

## Going deeper

Huang et al., "Machine Learning for Electronic Design Automation: A Survey," ACM TODAES (2021); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design: From Graph Partitioning to Timing Closure" (2nd ed., 2022), for the engines a model would assist.

problems.q:
A global placer spends most of its iterations waiting for a full global route to tell it where congestion is. Where can a learned model help most directly?

A) As a fast congestion estimate that the placer queries between expensive route runs

B) As a way to skip design rule checking

C) As a replacement for the final global router

D) As a replacement for the legalizer
problems.a: As a fast congestion estimate that the placer queries between expensive route runs
problems.e: Learning pays where an exact evaluation is slow and a fast, approximate answer is enough to steer a search. The router still produces the real routes.

problems.q:
A global placer spends most of its iterations waiting for a full global route to tell it where congestion is. Where can a learned model help most directly?

A) As a replacement for the legalizer

B) As a way to skip design rule checking

C) As a fast congestion estimate that the placer queries between expensive route runs

D) As a replacement for the final global router
problems.a: As a fast congestion estimate that the placer queries between expensive route runs
problems.e: Learning pays where an exact evaluation is slow and a fast, approximate answer is enough to steer a search. The router still produces the real routes.

problems.q:
Which property of a problem makes a learned heuristic most likely to help a classical algorithm?

A) Each instance is solved once and never resembles another

B) The algorithm faces many similar instances and makes repeated choices whose quality is hard to compute locally

C) The problem has a closed-form solution

D) The exact answer is cheaper than running a network
problems.a: The algorithm faces many similar instances and makes repeated choices whose quality is hard to compute locally
problems.e: Learning amortizes experience across similar instances. With a closed form or a cheap exact answer there is nothing to amortize.

problems.q:
A learned placer outputs coordinates with a few overlapping cells. Which component must still run?

A) A second learned placer

B) Nothing, because overlaps are cosmetic

C) A congestion predictor

D) A legalizer that snaps cells to rows and sites without overlap
problems.a: A legalizer that snaps cells to rows and sites without overlap
problems.e: Legality is a hard constraint enforced by an exact algorithm. A continuous or learned placement is never legal by construction.

problems.q:
Why can a timing predictor not replace static timing analysis at signoff?

A) Timing does not depend on the netlist

B) Its error has no guaranteed bound on an unseen design, while STA computes a conservative bound by construction

C) Predictors cannot output negative numbers

D) STA is faster than any predictor
problems.a: Its error has no guaranteed bound on an unseen design, while STA computes a conservative bound by construction
problems.e: STA's guarantee comes from propagating worst-case delays over every path. A model's error is only measured on its test set.

problems.q:
An LLM rewrites an RTL module to save area and reports that the behavior is unchanged. What establishes that claim?

A) Equivalence checking of the new module against the original

B) The code compiling without warnings

C) A second LLM agreeing

D) The model's confidence score
problems.a: Equivalence checking of the new module against the original
problems.e: Functional equivalence is a formal property. A combinational or sequential equivalence checker proves it; a model's statement does not.

problems.q:
A congestion predictor is wrong on 10 percent of tiles. In which use is that error rate least harmful?

A) Ordering which regions the placer spreads first, with a real global route afterwards

B) Choosing which nets need no routing

C) Deciding which tiles skip DRC

D) Reporting final overflow to signoff
problems.a: Ordering which regions the placer spreads first, with a real global route afterwards
problems.e: Errors in a heuristic ordering cost some runtime or quality, and the later exact step catches them. Errors in a decision that skips a check reach silicon.

problems.q:
A congestion predictor is wrong on 10 percent of tiles. In which use is that error rate least harmful?

A) Ordering which regions the placer spreads first, with a real global route afterwards

B) Deciding which tiles skip DRC

C) Reporting final overflow to signoff

D) Choosing which nets need no routing
problems.a: Ordering which regions the placer spreads first, with a real global route afterwards
problems.e: Errors in a heuristic ordering cost some runtime or quality, and the later exact step catches them. Errors in a decision that skips a check reach silicon.

problems.q:
Where should a learned component sit in a placer's architecture so that a bad model cannot produce an illegal result?

A) In the file writer, after legalization

B) In the strategy layer, feeding guidance to a core that enforces legality

C) In the row and site definitions

D) Inside the legalizer, replacing its overlap check
problems.a: In the strategy layer, feeding guidance to a core that enforces legality
problems.e: If the learned part only steers decisions and the core enforces invariants, the worst a bad model can do is a poor but legal result.

label: Labels from tool runs
prereqs: Where machine learning helps in EDA
lesson:
# Labels from tool runs

In EDA, a training label is almost never a human annotation. It is the output of a tool: the overflow a global router reports, the slack signoff STA computes, the violation count a DRC engine returns. Labels are therefore expensive, tied to one tool and setting, and correlated within a design. A tool designer must cost them before deciding a learned model is worth building.

## The cost of a label

Each label set costs a flow run. A congestion dataset of 20 designs with 10 parameter variants each needs 200 placement-and-route runs. At 6 machine-hours per run that is 1200 machine-hours; on 25 machines running in parallel the wall-clock time is $1200/25 = 48$ hours, or 2 days. Timing labels need routing, extraction and STA; DRC labels need detailed routing and a full rule check, which are slower still. Labels also inherit the tool's version and settings. If the router changes, labels made with the old router describe a different tool, and a model trained on them predicts the wrong outcome.

## Samples per run

One run yields many labels. A 400 by 400 um die cut into 4 um gcells has $100 \times 100 = 10{,}000$ gcells, so 200 runs give 2 million labeled gcells. The number is misleading. Gcells of one run share a netlist, a floorplan and a placement; gcells of variants of one design share most of that too. For generalization to a new design, the effective sample size is closer to the number of distinct designs than to the number of gcells. This is why random tile-level splits inflate test scores, and why datasets are judged by design diversity, not tile count.

## Break-even reuse

A predictor has a fixed cost, labels plus training, and a per-query saving: the tool run it replaces minus its own inference time. Suppose labels cost 1200 machine-hours and training 50 hours, so 1250 hours in all, and each query takes 0.05 hours instead of a 6-hour run. Each query saves 5.95 hours, and the smallest number of queries with net savings is $\lfloor 1250/5.95 \rfloor + 1 = 211$. If the exploration loop issues thousands of queries per project, the model pays. If it is used a few dozen times, or if every query still needs a confirming tool run, it never does.

## Going deeper

The CircuitNet dataset papers (Chai et al.) describe how flow runs become features and labels; the OpenROAD-flow-scripts documentation shows the runs such labels come from.

problems.q: To label a congestion dataset, a team runs 24 designs through the flow with 4 parameter variants each. One placement-and-global-route run takes 7 hours on one machine, and 32 machines run jobs in parallel. How many days of wall-clock time does labeling take? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Runs $= 24 \times 4 = 96$. Machine-hours $= 96 \times 7 = 672$. Wall-clock $= 672 / 32 / 24 = 0.88$ days.

problems.q: To label a congestion dataset, a team runs 14 designs through the flow with 8 parameter variants each. One placement-and-global-route run takes 9 hours on one machine, and 8 machines run jobs in parallel. How many days of wall-clock time does labeling take? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Runs $= 14 \times 8 = 112$. Machine-hours $= 112 \times 9 = 1008$. Wall-clock $= 1008 / 8 / 24 = 5.25$ days.

problems.q: To label a congestion dataset, a team runs 12 designs through the flow with 20 parameter variants each. One placement-and-global-route run takes 9 hours on one machine, and 64 machines run jobs in parallel. How many days of wall-clock time does labeling take? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Runs $= 12 \times 20 = 240$. Machine-hours $= 240 \times 9 = 2160$. Wall-clock $= 2160 / 64 / 24 = 1.41$ days.

problems.q: A congestion dataset labels every gcell of each routed run. A die is 600 by 400 um and a gcell is 10 by 10 um. The dataset holds 70 runs. How many labeled gcells does it contain?
problems.e: Per run: $(600/10)(400/10) = 60 \times 40 = 2400$ gcells. Times 70 runs: 168000. These labels are far from independent: gcells of one run share a design and a placement.

problems.q: A congestion dataset labels every gcell of each routed run. A die is 400 by 400 um and a gcell is 10 by 10 um. The dataset holds 99 runs. How many labeled gcells does it contain?
problems.e: Per run: $(400/10)(400/10) = 40 \times 40 = 1600$ gcells. Times 99 runs: 158400. These labels are far from independent: gcells of one run share a design and a placement.

problems.q: A congestion dataset labels every gcell of each routed run. A die is 600 by 300 um and a gcell is 10 by 10 um. The dataset holds 128 runs. How many labeled gcells does it contain?
problems.e: Per run: $(600/10)(300/10) = 60 \times 30 = 1800$ gcells. Times 128 runs: 230400. These labels are far from independent: gcells of one run share a design and a placement.

problems.q: Building a predictor costs 1700 machine-hours of tool runs for labels plus 137 hours of training. Afterwards each query takes 0.08 hours instead of the 4-hour tool run it replaces in an exploration loop. What is the smallest number of queries for which the predictor saves machine-hours overall? Give an integer.
problems.e: Savings per query $= 4 - 0.08 = 3.92$ hours. Fixed cost $= 1700 + 137 = 1837$ hours. The smallest $N$ with $N(3.92) > 1837$ is $\lfloor 1837 / 3.92 \rfloor + 1 = 469$. This assumes no query still needs a confirming tool run.

problems.q: Building a predictor costs 1689 machine-hours of tool runs for labels plus 107 hours of training. Afterwards each query takes 0.09 hours instead of the 15-hour tool run it replaces in an exploration loop. What is the smallest number of queries for which the predictor saves machine-hours overall? Give an integer.
problems.e: Savings per query $= 15 - 0.09 = 14.91$ hours. Fixed cost $= 1689 + 107 = 1796$ hours. The smallest $N$ with $N(14.91) > 1796$ is $\lfloor 1796 / 14.91 \rfloor + 1 = 121$. This assumes no query still needs a confirming tool run.

problems.q: Building a predictor costs 1689 machine-hours of tool runs for labels plus 109 hours of training. Afterwards each query takes 0.07 hours instead of the 11-hour tool run it replaces in an exploration loop. What is the smallest number of queries for which the predictor saves machine-hours overall? Give an integer.
problems.e: Savings per query $= 11 - 0.07 = 10.93$ hours. Fixed cost $= 1689 + 109 = 1798$ hours. The smallest $N$ with $N(10.93) > 1798$ is $\lfloor 1798 / 10.93 \rfloor + 1 = 165$. This assumes no query still needs a confirming tool run.

label: Netlists as graphs for learning
prereqs: Clique and star models of a net
lesson:
# Netlists as graphs for learning

A netlist is a hypergraph: a net joins any number of pins. Graph neural networks operate on ordinary graphs, so the first modeling decision is how to turn nets into edges. The choice decides how large the graph is, whether high-fanout nets swamp it, and whether the net itself survives as an object the model can attach features to.

## Clique, star and bipartite encodings

The clique model joins every pair of a net's pins, so a $p$-pin net becomes $\binom{p}{2}$ edges: a 5-pin net gives 10. The star model adds one node for the net and joins it to each pin, $p$ edges. The bipartite cell-net graph is the star model applied everywhere: one node per cell, one node per net, one edge per pin. Each preserves different information. The clique model loses the net as an entity and treats a 2-pin and a 50-pin connection between the same cells alike. The star and bipartite models keep the net, so net features such as fanout or bounding box have somewhere to live.

## Counting edges in a netlist

Edge counts add over nets. A netlist with nets of 3, 2, 3, 2 and 16 pins has clique edges $3 + 1 + 3 + 1 + 120 = 128$; the one 16-pin net contributes 120 of them. Under the bipartite model the same netlist has $3 + 2 + 3 + 2 + 16 = 26$ edges. Real designs have clock, reset and scan-enable nets with thousands of pins. A 5000-pin clock net alone has $\binom{5000}{2} \approx 12.5$ million clique edges, more than all the signal nets of a large block. Counting each net's edges separately gives a multigraph, since two cells can share several nets.

## Choosing an encoding

The ratio of clique edges to bipartite edges, $\sum \binom{p}{2} / \sum p$, measures how much the clique model inflates the graph; for nets of 2, 10, 2, 5 and 2 pins it is $58/21 \approx 2.76$, and it grows without bound with fanout. Most netlist GNNs therefore use a bipartite or star encoding, or keep cliques only for small nets and drop or star-expand large ones. Direction matters too: signals flow from driver to sinks, and timing tasks usually keep that direction, sometimes with separate driver and sink edge types. The encoding is a representation decision like any other in EDA: it fixes what the model can see and what it costs to compute.

## Going deeper

Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 2, on net models; Hamilton, "Graph Representation Learning" (2020), chapters 5 and 7.

problems.q: A net connects 15 pins (one driver and 14 sinks). Converting the netlist hypergraph to an ordinary graph with the clique model, how many edges does this net contribute?
problems.e: The clique model joins every pair of pins: $\binom{15}{2} = 15 \cdot 14 / 2 = 105$ edges.

problems.q: A net connects 16 pins (one driver and 15 sinks). Converting the hypergraph with the star model, which adds one new node for the net and joins it to every pin, how many edges does this net contribute?
problems.e: The star model adds a net node and one edge per pin: 16 edges, linear rather than quadratic in the pin count.

problems.q: A net connects 33 pins (one driver and 32 sinks). Converting the netlist hypergraph to an ordinary graph with the clique model, how many edges does this net contribute?
problems.e: The clique model joins every pair of pins: $\binom{33}{2} = 33 \cdot 32 / 2 = 528$ edges.

problems.q: A small netlist has nets with these pin counts: 4, 3, 2, 32, 5, 4. Using the clique model and counting each net's edges separately, how many edges does the graph have?
problems.e: Each net of $p$ pins gives $p(p-1)/2$ edges: 6 + 3 + 1 + 496 + 10 + 6, total 522. The 32-pin net alone gives 496.

problems.q: A small netlist has nets with these pin counts: 2, 4, 5, 2, 3, 32, 2, 2. Using the clique model and counting each net's edges separately, how many edges does the graph have?
problems.e: Each net of $p$ pins gives $p(p-1)/2$ edges: 1 + 6 + 10 + 1 + 3 + 496 + 1 + 1, total 519. The 32-pin net alone gives 496.

problems.q: A small netlist has nets with these pin counts: 2, 2, 3, 24, 3, 2, 4. Using the clique model and counting each net's edges separately, how many edges does the graph have?
problems.e: Each net of $p$ pins gives $p(p-1)/2$ edges: 1 + 1 + 3 + 276 + 3 + 1 + 6, total 291. The 24-pin net alone gives 276.

problems.q: A netlist has nets with pin counts 4, 4, 2, 2, 2, 16. A GNN can use the clique model (cells only, every pin pair joined) or a bipartite cell-net graph (one node per cell and per net, one edge per pin). What is the ratio of clique edges to bipartite edges? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Clique edges $= \sum p(p-1)/2 = 135$. Bipartite edges $= \sum p = 30$. Ratio $= 4.5$. The bipartite form keeps the net as an object and grows linearly with pins.

problems.q: A netlist has nets with pin counts 3, 4, 20, 5, 3, 5. A GNN can use the clique model (cells only, every pin pair joined) or a bipartite cell-net graph (one node per cell and per net, one edge per pin). What is the ratio of clique edges to bipartite edges? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Clique edges $= \sum p(p-1)/2 = 222$. Bipartite edges $= \sum p = 40$. Ratio $= 5.55$. The bipartite form keeps the net as an object and grows linearly with pins.

problems.q: A netlist has nets with pin counts 2, 2, 4, 2, 16. A GNN can use the clique model (cells only, every pin pair joined) or a bipartite cell-net graph (one node per cell and per net, one edge per pin). What is the ratio of clique edges to bipartite edges? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Clique edges $= \sum p(p-1)/2 = 129$. Bipartite edges $= \sum p = 26$. Ratio $= 4.96$. The bipartite form keeps the net as an object and grows linearly with pins.

label: Message passing and aggregation
lesson:
# Message passing and aggregation

A graph neural network layer updates each node from its own state and an aggregate of its neighbors' states. The aggregation is the part that handles graphs of any shape: it must accept any number of neighbors in any order. Sum, mean, max and degree-normalized sums each make different assumptions about what a netlist node's neighborhood means.

## Sum aggregation

One message-passing layer computes $h_v' = \sigma(W_s h_v + W_n \sum_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. Take scalar features and node $v$ with $h_v = 1$ and neighbors with features 2, -1 and 5. The sum is 6. With $W_s = 1$, $W_n = 0.5$ and ReLU, $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1 + 3) = 4$. Sum aggregation is permutation-invariant, so the order in which neighbors are listed does not matter, and it is the most expressive of the simple aggregators because it can count. It also scales with degree, so a cell on a 1000-pin net receives a message a thousand times larger than a cell on a 2-pin net.

## Mean and max aggregation

Mean aggregation divides the sum by the degree: the same node has mean $6/3 = 2$, and $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1 + 0.5 \cdot 2) = 2$. Mean is insensitive to degree, which stabilizes training on netlists with skewed fanout, but it cannot tell a node with one neighbor of feature 2 from one with three such neighbors. Max takes the largest neighbor feature, 5 here, and suits questions such as the latest arriving input of a gate, which is a max in static timing. A negative pre-activation is clipped by ReLU to zero, so the sign of the weights matters when checking a hand computation.

## Degree-normalized GCN layers

The graph convolutional network adds self-loops and normalizes each message by $\sqrt{\tilde d_u \tilde d_v}$, where $\tilde d$ is the degree plus one: $h_v' = W \sum_{u \in N(v) \cup \{v\}} h_u/\sqrt{\tilde d_u \tilde d_v}$. If $v$ has degree 3 ($\tilde d_v = 4$) and its neighbors have degrees 1, 2 and 3 with features 2, -1 and 5, the sum is $1/4 + 2/\sqrt{8} - 1/\sqrt{12} + 5/\sqrt{16} \approx 1.918$ for $h_v = 1$. Messages from high-degree neighbors are damped, which softens the effect of large nets. Stacking such layers repeatedly averages features, and after many layers node states become nearly indistinguishable, a failure called over-smoothing.

## Going deeper

Kipf and Welling, "Semi-Supervised Classification with Graph Convolutional Networks" (ICLR 2017); Hamilton, Ying and Leskovec, "Inductive Representation Learning on Large Graphs" (NeurIPS 2017).

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 6 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–4, 2–3, 4–5, 4–6. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 4$, $h_{2} = 1$, $h_{3} = 3$, $h_{4} = 9$, $h_{5} = 7$, $h_{6} = 2$. One message-passing layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1\,h_v + 2\sum_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{4}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Neighbors of node 4: 1, 5, 6, with feature sum 13. $\mathrm{ReLU}(1 \cdot 9 + 2 \cdot 13) = 35$.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 5 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–3, 3–4, 3–5. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 8$, $h_{2} = 9$, $h_{3} = 6$, $h_{4} = 0$, $h_{5} = 5$. One message-passing layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1\,h_v + 3\sum_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{3}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Neighbors of node 3: 1, 4, 5, with feature sum 13. $\mathrm{ReLU}(1 \cdot 6 + 3 \cdot 13) = 45$.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 6 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–5, 2–3, 2–4, 2–5, 2–6. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 8$, $h_{2} = 8$, $h_{3} = 8$, $h_{4} = 8$, $h_{5} = 4$, $h_{6} = -2$. One message-passing layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1\,h_v + 1\sum_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{2}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Neighbors of node 2: 1, 3, 4, 5, 6, with feature sum 26. $\mathrm{ReLU}(1 \cdot 8 + 1 \cdot 26) = 34$.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 5 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–3, 1–4, 2–4, 2–5, 3–5. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 2$, $h_{2} = -3$, $h_{3} = 2$, $h_{4} = -3$, $h_{5} = 9$. One layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(2\,h_v + (-2) \cdot \mathrm{mean}_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{5}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Node 5 has 2 neighbors with sum -1, so the mean is -0.5. Pre-activation $2 \cdot 9 + (-2) \cdot (-0.5) = 19$, and ReLU gives 19.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 5 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–5, 2–3, 2–4, 4–5. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 6$, $h_{2} = -1$, $h_{3} = 6$, $h_{4} = -1$, $h_{5} = 5$. One layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}((-1)\,h_v + (-2) \cdot \mathrm{mean}_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{5}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Node 5 has 2 neighbors with sum 5, so the mean is 2.5. Pre-activation $(-1) \cdot 5 + (-2) \cdot 2.5 = -10$, and ReLU gives 0.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 6 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–4, 2–5, 3–6, 4–5. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 1$, $h_{2} = 5$, $h_{3} = 6$, $h_{4} = -2$, $h_{5} = -3$, $h_{6} = -3$. One layer computes $h_v' = \mathrm{ReLU}(1\,h_v + 1 \cdot \mathrm{mean}_{u \in N(v)} h_u)$. What is $h_{1}'$? Round to 2 decimal places.
problems.e: Node 1 has 2 neighbors with sum 11, so the mean is 5.5. Pre-activation $1 \cdot 1 + 1 \cdot 5.5 = 6.5$, and ReLU gives 6.5.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 5 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–3, 2–3, 2–5, 3–4, 4–5. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 8$, $h_{2} = 6$, $h_{3} = 7$, $h_{4} = 6$, $h_{5} = 7$. A GCN layer with self loops computes $h_v' = 2\sum_{u \in N(v) \cup \{v\}} h_u / \sqrt{\tilde{d}_u \tilde{d}_v}$, where $\tilde{d}$ is the degree plus one. No activation is applied. What is $h_{2}'$? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: $\tilde{d}_{2} = 4$. The sum is $6/4 + 8/\sqrt{12} + 7/\sqrt{16} + 7/\sqrt{12} = 7.5801$, times 2 gives 15.16. High-degree neighbors are damped by their larger $\tilde{d}_u$.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 6 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–4, 1–5, 2–3, 3–6, 5–6. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = 4$, $h_{2} = -2$, $h_{3} = 9$, $h_{4} = 8$, $h_{5} = 1$, $h_{6} = 7$. A GCN layer with self loops computes $h_v' = 3\sum_{u \in N(v) \cup \{v\}} h_u / \sqrt{\tilde{d}_u \tilde{d}_v}$, where $\tilde{d}$ is the degree plus one. No activation is applied. What is $h_{1}'$? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: $\tilde{d}_{1} = 4$. The sum is $4/4 + (-2)/\sqrt{12} + 8/\sqrt{8} + 1/\sqrt{12} = 3.5398$, times 3 gives 10.619. High-degree neighbors are damped by their larger $\tilde{d}_u$.

problems.q: A netlist graph has nodes 1 to 6 and undirected edges 1–2, 1–3, 1–4, 1–6, 2–5, 4–6. Each node carries a scalar feature: $h_{1} = -1$, $h_{2} = 3$, $h_{3} = 5$, $h_{4} = 2$, $h_{5} = 2$, $h_{6} = -1$. A GCN layer with self loops computes $h_v' = 2\sum_{u \in N(v) \cup \{v\}} h_u / \sqrt{\tilde{d}_u \tilde{d}_v}$, where $\tilde{d}$ is the degree plus one. No activation is applied. What is $h_{1}'$? Round to 3 decimal places.
problems.e: $\tilde{d}_{1} = 5$. The sum is $(-1)/5 + 3/\sqrt{15} + 5/\sqrt{10} + 2/\sqrt{15} + (-1)/\sqrt{15} = 2.4139$, times 2 gives 4.828. High-degree neighbors are damped by their larger $\tilde{d}_u$.

label: Graph neural networks on netlists
lesson:
# Graph neural networks on netlists

Stacking message-passing layers gives a GNN, which maps a netlist to embeddings per cell, net or pin, and from them to predictions such as slack, congestion or a partition label. Three properties decide whether a GNN fits an EDA task: how far information travels, whether the path it must travel is short enough, and whether the model applies to netlists it has never seen.

## The receptive field

After $k$ layers, a node's embedding depends exactly on the nodes within $k$ hops: its $k$-hop neighborhood. A one-layer GNN sees direct neighbors, a two-layer GNN their neighbors as well. Computing this is a breadth-first search to depth $k$. If a gate has three neighbors in the cell graph and each of them has two further neighbors, a two-layer embedding of the gate depends on $1 + 3 + 6 = 10$ cells. The receptive field is a hard limit: if the label depends on a node outside it, no amount of training can find that dependence, and the model learns a correlation instead.

## Depth versus logic depth

Timing is a long-range property. A path from a launching flip-flop through 9 gates to a capturing flip-flop has 11 cells and 10 nets. In a bipartite cell-net graph each net costs two hops, cell to net and net to cell, so the capturing flop is 20 hops from the launching one, and a GNN needs 20 layers before one can influence the other. Deep GNNs over-smooth and are slow, so timing models usually do something else: they propagate along the timing graph in topological order, one level per step, so that arrival-like features accumulate along paths as they do in STA.

## Inductive models and parameter count

A GNN's weights are shared by every node, so its parameter count does not depend on the netlist size. A model with 16 input features, width 64, three layers each with a self matrix, a neighbor matrix and a bias, and a linear readout has $(2 \cdot 16 \cdot 64 + 64) + 2(2 \cdot 64^2 + 64) + 65 = 18{,}689$ parameters, whether it runs on a 10-thousand-cell or a 10-million-cell netlist. That makes the model inductive: it applies to unseen netlists. It does not make it accurate on them. Generalization depends on whether the new netlist's neighborhoods look like the training ones.

# Heterogeneous circuit graphs

A netlist has different kinds of objects (cells, nets, pins, macros, I/O ports) and different kinds of relations (drives, feeds, belongs to, is near). A homogeneous GNN forces all of them into one node type and one edge type. A heterogeneous GNN gives each type its own features and each relation its own weights, at a parameter cost the designer must budget.

## Relation-specific weights

A relational layer computes $h_v' = \sigma(W_0 h_v + \sum_r \sum_{u \in N_r(v)} W_r h_u / c_{v,r} + b)$, with one matrix $W_r$ per relation $r$ and a normalizing constant $c_{v,r}$ such as the number of $r$-neighbors. With 4 relations (cell-drives-net, net-feeds-cell and their reverses) and width 64, one layer has $(4 + 1) \cdot 64^2 + 64 = 20{,}544$ parameters. Parameters grow linearly with the number of relations, so schemas with many relation types share weights through a basis decomposition, writing each $W_r$ as a combination of a few shared matrices.

## Per-type input encoders

Node types carry different raw features. A cell has a one-hot cell type, drive strength and area; a net has fanout and bounding-box size; a pin has capacitance and direction. A separate linear encoder per type maps each into a shared width $d$, costing $f_t d + d$ parameters for a type with $f_t$ features. With 24 cell features, 6 net features, 4 pin features and $d = 64$, the encoders cost $(24 + 6 + 4) \cdot 64 + 3 \cdot 64 = 2368$ parameters. One-hot cell types tie the model to one library; features computed from Liberty data, such as input capacitance and drive resistance, transfer better across libraries.

## Typed edges and direction

In a heterogeneous netlist graph, a net with one driver and $s$ sinks contributes one drives edge and $s$ feeds edges. Seven nets with fanouts 6, 3, 2, 6, 4, 2 and 3 give 7 drives edges and 26 feeds edges. Adding a reverse relation for each lets messages flow from sinks back to drivers, doubling the total to 66. Direction carries meaning: timing propagates driver to sink and required times flow back, so forward and reverse relations should have separate weights. A homogeneous undirected graph would merge the two and lose that distinction.

## Going deeper

Schlichtkrull et al., "Modeling Relational Data with Graph Convolutional Networks" (ESWC 2018); Hamilton, "Graph Representation Learning" (2020), chapter 5.

lesson:
# Netlist size and fanout skew in GNNs

Netlists are hard for GNNs for two reasons that most benchmark graphs do not share: they are large, with millions of cells, and their degree distribution is extremely skewed, with clock, reset and scan nets touching thousands of pins. Both shape how a netlist GNN is trained and what it can compute in one pass.

## Messages per layer

In a full-graph layer every edge carries a message in each direction it is used. A bipartite cell-net graph has one edge per pin, so a block with 10,000 signal nets averaging 3 pins plus one 5000-pin clock net has $30{,}000 + 5000 = 35{,}000$ edges and sends 70,000 messages per layer if messages flow both ways. Memory for a layer scales with edges times width, plus stored activations for backpropagation. A design with tens of millions of pins exceeds one GPU's memory for full-graph training, which forces mini-batching. The clock net alone carries one seventh of those messages, from a single net among ten thousand.

## Neighbor sampling

Mini-batch training computes embeddings only for a batch of target nodes, and for each one samples at most $s$ neighbors per layer. The computation tree of one target then has at most $1 + s + s^2 + \dots + s^L$ nodes; with $s = 10$ and $L = 2$ that is 111. Without the cap, a target adjacent to the clock net would pull in all 5000 of its pins at the first hop. Sampling makes training feasible but adds variance, and it changes what the model sees: an aggregate over 10 of 5000 sinks is a noisy estimate of the full aggregate.

## When one net dominates

Under the clique model, a 5000-pin net contributes $\binom{5000}{2} = 12{,}497{,}500$ edges. If the other 10,000 nets add 30,000 edges, the clock net is $12{,}497{,}500/12{,}527{,}500 \approx 99.8$ percent of the graph. Its messages swamp every cell it touches, and every cell becomes two hops from every other. Practical netlist GNNs drop such nets, cap their fanout, star-expand them, or model them separately; clock nets are usually handled by clock-tree synthesis anyway, so their logical connectivity carries little information for tasks such as congestion. The decision is part of the representation, so it should be recorded with the dataset and applied identically at training and inference time.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Congestion prediction

Routing congestion is known only after global routing, but the placer needs it while cells can still move. Congestion prediction maps placement-stage features to the router's overflow map, usually as an image-to-image problem on the gcell grid. The fast estimate RUDY is both a baseline and a standard input feature, and the evaluation metric decides whether the model helps where it matters.

## RUDY as a feature

RUDY (rectangular uniform wire density) spreads each net's estimated wirelength, its half-perimeter $w + h$, uniformly over its bounding box. The density it adds at every point of the box is $(w + h)/(wh)$, in um of wire per square um. A 10 by 20 um net adds $30/200 = 0.15$ per um; a 2 by 2 um net adds $4/4 = 1$, so tight pin clusters show up as hot. RUDY is cheap, needs no router, and correlates with routing demand, which is why learned congestion models take it as an input channel together with pin density, cell density and macro blockage maps.

## From nets to a tile map

A gcell's RUDY value sums each net's density times the area of overlap between the net's box and the gcell, divided by the gcell area. For a 10 by 10 um tile fully inside the 10 by 20 um box above, the net contributes $0.15 \times 100 = 15$ um of wire, a density of 0.15. A second net of density 0.4 overlapping 25 square um adds 10 um, raising the tile to $25/100 = 0.25$. Rasterizing every feature this way turns the placement into a stack of 2-D maps, and the router's overflow per gcell into a target map. A convolutional encoder-decoder then learns the image-to-image mapping, which captures spatial context that RUDY alone ignores, such as detours around macros.

## Judging a congestion map

Map-wide metrics can hide the failures that matter. NRMSE divides the root-mean-square error by the range of the true values. True overflows 0, 2, 4 and 8 against predictions 1, 2, 3 and 6 give squared errors summing to 6, RMSE $\sqrt{6/4} = 1.22$ and NRMSE $1.22/8 = 0.153$. Most tiles are uncongested, so a model that predicts low everywhere scores well while missing the few hot tiles a placer must spread. Useful evaluations add per-tile classification metrics on hotspots, ranking metrics such as correlation of hot regions, and above all whether the placer's routed result improves when it uses the prediction.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Timing prediction

Before routing, the placer and optimizer see only estimated wire parasitics, so their slack differs from signoff slack after routing. Pre-route timing prediction learns the post-route slack, or the net and arc delays, from placement-stage features. It is a regression problem, but the metric that matters is not the average error: it is whether the prediction gets the critical endpoints right.

## Mean absolute error

Given actual post-route slacks $y_i$ and predictions $\hat y_i$ at $n$ endpoints, the mean absolute error is $\frac{1}{n}\sum |y_i - \hat y_i|$. For actual slacks -10, 5 and 20 ps and predictions -4, -2 and 26 ps, the errors are 6, 7 and 6 ps and the MAE is 6.33 ps. MAE is in the units of the label and is robust to a few large errors, but it weights every endpoint equally. In a design with 100,000 endpoints most are far from critical, so a low MAE can coexist with large errors on the few hundred endpoints that decide closure.

## The coefficient of determination

$R^2 = 1 - \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2 / \sum (y_i - \bar y)^2$ compares the residual error with the spread of the labels. In the example, $\bar y = 5$, the total sum of squares is $225 + 0 + 225 = 450$ and the residual sum is $36 + 49 + 36 = 121$, so $R^2 = 1 - 121/450 = 0.731$. $R^2$ rewards a model for following a wide spread of slacks, which is easy when slacks range over hundreds of picoseconds. A model with $R^2 = 0.95$ over all endpoints can still be poor in the narrow band near zero slack, which is the band an optimizer acts on.

## Getting the violation status right

An optimizer's decision at an endpoint depends on the sign of slack: fix it or leave it. Counting endpoints where the predicted sign differs from the actual sign measures the errors that change behavior. In the example, endpoint 2 has actual slack 5 ps and predicted -2 ps, so one endpoint flips: the optimizer would waste effort on a passing path. lesson:
# DRC hotspot prediction

A DRC hotspot predictor flags gcells likely to contain design-rule violations after detailed routing, so the placer or router can act early. It is a classification problem with extreme class imbalance: violations sit in a tiny fraction of gcells. That makes accuracy meaningless and makes precision depend on how rare hotspots are in the design at hand.

## Precision and recall

Compare the flagged gcells with the DRC engine's report. True positives (TP) are flagged gcells with violations, false positives (FP) are flagged clean gcells, and false negatives (FN) are violating gcells not flagged. Precision is $TP/(TP + FP)$, the fraction of flags that are real; recall is $TP/(TP + FN)$, the fraction of real hotspots caught. With 40 true flags, 60 false alarms and 20 misses, precision is 40 percent and recall 66.7 percent. Accuracy would count the many true negatives too: on 250,000 gcells, flagging nothing scores over 99.9 percent accuracy while catching no hotspot at all.

## The F1 score

F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall, $2PR/(P + R)$, which equals $2TP/(2TP + FP + FN)$. In the example, $F_1 = 80/(80 + 60 + 20) = 0.5$. True negatives never appear, so F1 is not inflated by the sea of clean gcells. The harmonic mean is pulled toward the smaller of the two, so a model cannot score well by maximizing one and ignoring the other. F1 still hides the trade-off a tool designer cares about: a router may tolerate many false alarms (extra spreading costs a little wirelength) but not misses, in which case recall at a fixed false-alarm budget is the better target.

## Precision depends on prevalence

Recall and the false-positive rate are properties of the classifier; precision also depends on how common hotspots are. Per gcell, the expected true flags are recall times prevalence and the false flags are the false-positive rate times one minus prevalence. A classifier with recall 0.9 and false-positive rate 0.01 on a design where 0.5 percent of gcells are hotspots gives true flags 0.0045 and false flags 0.00995, so precision is $0.0045/0.01445 = 31$ percent. The same classifier on a design with 5 percent hotspots reaches 83 percent. A precision reported on one design does not transfer to a cleaner one.

label: IR-drop prediction
lesson:
# IR-drop prediction

IR drop is the voltage lost across the resistance of the power grid as cells draw current. Computing it means solving a large resistive network, and dynamic analysis repeats that over many time steps and vectors. Learned IR-drop predictors map power and grid feature maps to a drop map, trained on solver results. The metric that matters is whether the worst drops and the hotspots are found.

## What the solver computes

The label comes from a power-grid solver, which applies Kirchhoff's laws to the grid. On a single strap fed from a pad, each segment carries the current of every tap beyond it. With segment resistance 0.1 ohm and taps drawing 10, 20 and 30 mA from the pad outward, the segments carry 60, 50 and 30 mA, and the drop at the last tap is $0.1(60 + 50 + 30) = 14$ mV (ohm times mA is mV). A real grid is a mesh solved as a sparse linear system $G v = i$ with millions of nodes. The predictor learns how current maps and grid structure turn into drops, the mapping the solver computes exactly.

## Errors in the worst drop

Signoff checks the worst drop against a budget, so the error in the predicted maximum matters more than the average error. If the true worst drop is 57 mV and the predicted worst is 68 mV, the error is $11/57 = 19.3$ percent. The two maxima need not occur in the same tile. A model can predict the right worst value in the wrong place, which passes this metric and still misleads a designer about where to add straps. Evaluations therefore report the maximum error, the location of the predicted hotspot and the per-tile error, rather than one aggregate number.

## Hotspot recall

Designers act on tiles above a drop threshold, so IR-drop predictors are also judged as hotspot detectors. Recall is the fraction of tiles truly above the threshold that the model also places above it. If three tiles exceed 45 mV in the solver result and the model puts two of them above 45 mV, recall is 67 percent. A missed hotspot is the costly error: no one re-simulates a region the model called safe. In a flow, the predictor is a fast mode for early power-grid planning and for screening many vectors, and the solver still produces the signoff result.

## Going deeper

label: Datasets for ML in EDA
lesson:
# Datasets for ML in EDA

Progress on learned EDA models depends on shared data, and EDA data is scarce: designs are proprietary, labels need expensive tool runs, and results depend on the node and the flow. Open datasets such as CircuitNet package flow runs as features and labels. Knowing how they are built tells a tool designer what a reported result on them does and does not show.

## What a dataset contains

An ML-for-EDA dataset pairs inputs a tool sees early with labels a tool computes later. CircuitNet, for example, provides layout-derived feature maps (cell density, pin density, RUDY, macro regions) with labels such as routing congestion, DRC violations and IR drop, produced by running designs through physical-design flows under many settings. Synthesis datasets such as OpenABC-D pair and-inverter graphs with the QoR that ABC reports after many recipes. The input representation decides the task's form: grids give image-to-image problems, netlists give graph problems. Each label is only as trustworthy as the run that produced it, so the dataset's flow, node and tool versions belong with the data.

## How splits mislead

Because labels are costly and open designs few, datasets grow by running variants of a small number of designs. Samples from one design share netlist structure, floorplan and flow style. A random split of tiles or runs puts the same design in training and test, so the test score measures recognition of seen designs. The honest split holds out whole designs, and the effective sample size is the number of distinct designs. Labels also carry their tool: a model trained on labels from one router, rule deck and node predicts that combination, and must be re-evaluated before use with another.

## Comparable results

A benchmark is the data, the split and the metric together. Two papers that use the same dataset with different splits, metrics or preprocessing report incomparable numbers. Reproducibility also needs the flow scripts and parameters that produced each label, so that others can regenerate and audit them. A tool designer reading a result on an open dataset should ask which node and PDK the labels came from, whether the split held out designs, and whether the gain was measured in a flow, such as improved routed congestion, or only as prediction error.

## Going deeper

The CircuitNet dataset papers (Chai et al.); Chowdhury et al., "OpenABC-D: A Large-Scale Dataset for Machine Learning Guided Integrated Circuit Synthesis" (2021).

label: EDA problems as Markov decision processes
prereqs: Where machine learning helps in EDA
lesson:
# EDA problems as Markov decision processes

Reinforcement learning applies when a design task is a sequence of decisions whose quality shows up later: place one macro, then the next; apply one synthesis transform, then the next. Casting the task as a Markov decision process means choosing states, actions, rewards and a discount, and those choices decide whether the agent can learn anything at all.

## Returns and discounting

An agent at step $t$ receives reward $r_t$, and its return from step 0 is $G_0 = \sum_t \gamma^t r_t$ with discount $\gamma \le 1$. For a synthesis agent whose rewards after four commands are 1, -4, 2 and 2 (node reductions, in hundreds), $\gamma = 0.9$ gives $1 - 3.6 + 1.62 + 1.458 = 0.478$. The discount says how much later rewards count. In an EDA episode, later steps often matter as much as early ones, because the final QoR is what is measured, so a small discount can make the agent short-sighted and favor transforms that help now and hurt the final result.

## Sparse terminal rewards

Many EDA objectives are known only at the end: a placement's wirelength and congestion are evaluated after all macros are placed. With reward 0 at every step and $-c$ at the last of $M$ steps, the return from step 0 is $-c\gamma^{M-1}$. With $M = 100$ and $\gamma = 0.99$, the terminal reward is scaled by $0.99^{99} = 0.37$; with $\gamma = 0.95$ by 0.006, so early macros receive almost no signal. Placement formulations therefore often use $\gamma = 1$, and some add intermediate rewards, such as partial wirelength, which shapes learning but must not change which final placements are best.

## Value estimates and TD error

A critic learns $V(s)$, the expected return from state $s$, to reduce the variance of policy updates. After one transition the temporal-difference error is $\delta = r + \gamma V(s') - V(s)$. With $V(s) = 2$, an intermediate density penalty $r = -1$, $\gamma = 0.9$ and $V(s') = 4$, $\delta = -1 + 3.6 - 2 = 0.6$: the move went better than expected, and actor-critic methods raise the probability of that action. In EDA the state is large (a partial placement plus a netlist), so $V$ is a neural network, often on top of a GNN encoder, and its errors become noise in the policy gradient.

## Going deeper

Sutton and Barto, "Reinforcement Learning: An Introduction" (2nd ed., 2018), chapters 3 and 6.

label: Reinforcement learning for placement
prereqs: EDA problems as Markov decision processes
lesson:
# Reinforcement learning for placement

The best-known RL application in EDA treats macro placement as a game: an agent places macros one at a time on a grid, a conventional method places the standard cells, and a proxy cost scores the result. Understanding exactly what the agent decides, what the reward measures and what it leaves out is the basis for judging any claim about the method.

## Macro placement as a sequence

The state is the netlist plus the partial placement; the action is the grid cell where the next macro goes, typically ordered by size; the episode ends when all macros are placed. Illegal actions, positions that overlap a placed macro or leave the canvas, are masked so the policy can only choose legal cells. Standard cells, which number in the millions, are not placed by the agent; a separate conventional placer, such as a force-directed method, places them for evaluating the reward. A graph neural network encodes the netlist and the placement for the policy and value networks, which lets one model be pretrained across blocks and fine-tuned on a new one.

## The proxy cost

Routing and signoff timing are too slow to run for every episode, so the reward is the negative of a proxy cost, $\mathrm{WL} + \lambda_c C + \lambda_d D$, combining normalized wirelength, congestion and density. A placement with $\mathrm{WL} = 0.8$, $C = 1.2$ and $D = 0.9$ and weights $\lambda_c = \lambda_d = 0.5$ costs $0.8 + 0.6 + 0.45 = 1.85$. The weights set which failure the agent avoids most. No term is routed timing or power, so a lower proxy cost is a hypothesis about a better chip, to be checked after routing.

## Judging an RL placement result

Three questions decide whether an RL placement result is meaningful. First, does a strong non-learned optimizer, such as simulated annealing on the same proxy and grid with matched compute, reach the same cost? If so, the gain comes from the formulation, not from learning. Second, does the proxy track post-route metrics? A lower proxy with worse routed timing shows the agent exploited the proxy. Third, what did the agent receive: pretraining data, initial placement information from another tool, compute? In the four-layer engine model the policy sits in the strategy layer, proposing macro positions that the core legalizes and the downstream flow evaluates.

## Going deeper

Mirhoseini et al., "A graph placement methodology for fast chip design," Nature (2021); Kahng, Lienig, Markov and Hu, "VLSI Physical Design" (2nd ed., 2022), chapter 4, on macro placement.

label: The RL macro-placement reproducibility debate
lesson:
# The RL macro-placement reproducibility debate

The RL macro placer published in Nature in 2021 became a case study in how ML results in EDA should be evaluated. Independent groups ran the released code on open designs and reported that classical methods matched or beat it; the original authors disputed how the reproductions were run. A tool designer does not need to settle the dispute to learn from what each side measured.

## The original claim

The paper described an RL agent with a graph-based encoder that places macros sequentially, pretrained across many blocks and fine-tuned on new ones, and reported quality comparable to or better than human experts in much less time, evaluated on Google's production blocks. Google released an open-source implementation, Circuit Training. Because the evaluation blocks and parts of the flow were proprietary, outsiders could not rerun the original experiments; they could only run the released method on other designs, which is a different experiment. Results were reported on both proxy cost and post-route metrics, and which of the two a comparison uses changes its conclusion.

## What the critiques measured

An academic assessment ran Circuit Training on open designs and enablements and compared it with simulated annealing, analytical placers, a commercial macro placer and human placements. Its questions were concrete: with comparable inputs and evaluation, does the learned policy beat strong non-learned optimizers; how well does the proxy cost track routed timing, power and wirelength; does placement information produced by a commercial tool and fed to the method account for part of its quality. Proponents replied that the reproductions differed from the published method, for example in pretraining and compute. Both arguments are about accounting: what was run, with what inputs and budget, on which metric.

## Lessons for evaluation

The debate lasted because the evidence was not on shared ground. The fix is a standard for ML-in-EDA claims: open designs and flows that anyone can rerun; strong baselines on the same objective with matched compute; several seeds and several designs, since one run on one design says nothing about variance; downstream metrics, not only the proxy that was optimized; and ablations of every input that could carry information from another optimizer. A team considering a learned macro placer should measure post-route PPA and runtime on its own blocks against its current method, which is the only result that answers its question.

## Going deeper

lesson:
# Reinforcement learning for synthesis recipes

Logic synthesis in ABC runs a recipe: a sequence of transforms such as balance, rewrite, refactor and resub on an and-inverter graph. Which sequence works best depends on the circuit. RL and bandit methods search recipe space using the tool's own measurements as reward, and the choice of reward decides whether the found recipe helps after technology mapping.

## The recipe space

With $K$ transforms and recipes of length $L$, repeats allowed, there are $K^L$ recipes. Six transforms and length 10 give $6^{10} = 60{,}466{,}176$ recipes, far too many to try when each takes seconds to minutes on a large circuit. Transforms do not commute, and their effect depends on the current graph, so the problem is sequential: the state is the current AIG (or features of it), the action is the next transform, and the episode ends after $L$ steps. A learned policy generalizes across circuits only if its state features capture what makes a transform useful.

## A Q-learning update

Tabular or approximate Q-learning keeps $Q(s, a)$, the expected return of applying transform $a$ in state $s$. After applying rewrite with $Q(s, \text{rewrite}) = 0.5$ and receiving reward $r = 2$, with the best next-state value 1, learning rate 0.1 and $\gamma = 0.9$, the target is $2 + 0.9 \cdot 1 = 2.9$ and the update gives $0.5 + 0.1(2.9 - 0.5) = 0.74$. Real states are AIGs, so $Q$ is a neural network over graph features, and each reward needs a tool call, which keeps the number of training episodes small.

## Shaping the reward

A typical reward combines normalized improvements in AIG node count and logic depth, $r = w(A_{\mathrm{prev}} - A)/A_0 + (1 - w)(D_{\mathrm{prev}} - D)/D_0$. Both are proxies. AIG node count and depth are cheap to measure but do not determine mapped area and delay, which depend on the cell library and the mapper. A recipe that minimizes nodes can map worse than one that keeps useful structure. Sound evaluations report mapped area and delay, or post-synthesis timing, compare with standard recipes such as the ones ABC ships, and count the tool calls spent in search, since a tuned recipe found by brute force on one circuit is not a learned result.

## Going deeper

Hosny et al., "DRiLLS: Deep Reinforcement Learning for Logic Synthesis" (ASP-DAC 2020); Mishchenko, Chatterjee and Brayton, "DAG-Aware AIG Rewriting" (DAC 2006), for the transforms being sequenced.

label: Speedup accounting for surrogates
lesson:
# Speedup accounting for surrogates

A surrogate is a fast model that stands in for an expensive evaluation, such as SPICE, routing or signoff STA, inside a search loop. Its value is the end-to-end speedup of the loop, not its own inference speed. That speedup must include the evaluations that still run for verification, the cost of building the surrogate, and the part of the flow it does not touch.

## Screening plus verification

Suppose a loop scores $N = 1000$ candidate sizings, SPICE takes 60 minutes each and the surrogate 1 minute, and the top 5 percent by surrogate score are re-run in SPICE before anything is accepted. Without the surrogate the loop costs $1000 \times 60 = 60{,}000$ minutes. With it the loop costs $1000 \times 1 + 0.05 \times 1000 \times 60 = 4000$ minutes, a speedup of 15. The verification term dominates: as the surrogate gets faster the speedup approaches $1/0.05 = 20$, never more. The fraction sent to verification is a policy decision, and shrinking it trades safety for speed.

## Amortizing the build cost

The surrogate itself costs labels and training. If building it took 200 machine-hours (12,000 minutes) and it serves 4 exploration campaigns, each campaign carries 3000 minutes of build cost, and the loop above costs $4000 + 3000 = 7000$ minutes, a speedup of $60{,}000/7000 = 8.6$. Served once, the same surrogate gives $60{,}000/16{,}000 = 3.75$. A reported speedup that leaves out data generation and training answers a different question: how fast the model runs once it exists. A tool designer needs the amortized number, which depends on how often the model is reused before the design, node or tool changes enough to invalidate it.

## The whole-flow bound

Accelerating one step speeds up the flow only in proportion to that step's share of runtime, as Amdahl's law states. If a step is a fraction $p$ of flow runtime and becomes $s$ times faster, the flow speedup is $1/((1 - p) + p/s)$. With $p = 0.6$ and $s = 10$ the flow is $1/(0.4 + 0.06) = 2.17$ times faster, and no surrogate can exceed $1/0.4 = 2.5$. Claims of orders-of-magnitude speedup for one analysis step are therefore compatible with modest flow-level gains. The step a surrogate replaces must also not be the one whose result the next stage depends on exactly.

## Going deeper

Forrester, Sobester and Keane, "Engineering Design via Surrogate Modelling" (2008), chapters 1 and 2.

label: Surrogates and active learning
lesson:
# Surrogates and active learning

Labels for an EDA surrogate cost tool runs, so which points to label matters as much as how many. Active learning lets the model choose: it labels the candidates it is least sure about, where a label teaches it most. Uncertainty from an ensemble or a Gaussian process drives the choice, and retraining overhead decides whether the saving is real.

## Ensemble disagreement

An ensemble of models trained on different subsets or seeds gives several predictions for one candidate. Their spread estimates the model's uncertainty there. If four surrogates predict a sizing's phase margin as 60, 64, 58 and 62 degrees, the mean is 61 and the population variance is $(1 + 9 + 9 + 1)/4 = 5$ square degrees. Disagreement is high where training data is sparse or the function changes fast, and low where the models have seen similar points. It measures the model's own uncertainty, not noise in the simulator, and it can be low and wrong together if every member shares the same bias.

## Uncertainty sampling

The simplest active-learning rule, uncertainty sampling, sends the unlabeled candidate with the largest predictive variance to the expensive tool. Among five candidate paths, if three ensemble members agree closely on four of them and spread over 11 ps on the fifth, the fifth goes to the timer next, whatever its predicted slack. Pure uncertainty sampling explores; it does not care whether a point is relevant to the design goal. Variants weight uncertainty by relevance, for example preferring uncertain points near zero slack or near a specification boundary, and batch versions pick several diverse points per round so the tool runs in parallel.

## Counting the saving

Suppose random sampling needs 2000 labeled runs to reach a target error and active learning needs 600. At 4 machine-hours per label, labels saved are worth $1400 \times 4 = 5600$ hours. Active learning retrains after each batch; with batches of 50 and 2 hours per retrain it runs $\lceil 600/50 \rceil = 12$ rounds at 24 hours, so the net saving is 5576 hours. Small batches choose better points but retrain more often and serialize the tool runs. The labels it collects are also biased toward hard regions, so a model evaluated on them looks worse than it is, and a separate random test set is needed to measure accuracy.

## Going deeper

Settles, "Active Learning Literature Survey" (University of Wisconsin-Madison, 2009); Rasmussen and Williams, "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning" (2006), chapter 2.

prereqs: The inverse of a two-by-two matrix
lesson:
# Gaussian-process posteriors

A Gaussian process is the standard surrogate in Bayesian optimization for analog sizing and flow tuning, because it gives a mean and a calibrated uncertainty at every point from a handful of expensive runs. Its posterior has closed-form mean and variance. Computing them for one and two observations shows exactly how data pulls the prediction and shrinks the uncertainty.

## The posterior mean

A GP prior has mean $m$ and kernel $k(x, x')$, for example the squared exponential $\sigma_f^2 \exp(-(x - x')^2/(2\ell^2))$. After one noisy observation $y_1$ at $x_1$ with noise variance $\sigma_n^2$, the posterior mean at $x^*$ is $\mu^* = m + \frac{k(x^*, x_1)}{k(x_1, x_1) + \sigma_n^2}(y_1 - m)$. With $m = 0$, $\sigma_f^2 = 1$, $\ell = 1$, $\sigma_n^2 = 0.1$, $y_1 = 2$ at $x_1 = 0$ and $x^* = 1$: $k(x^*, x_1) = e^{-0.5} = 0.607$, so $\mu^* = 0.607 \cdot 2/1.1 = 1.10$. Far from the data the kernel decays and the mean returns to the prior.

## The posterior variance

The posterior variance at $x^*$ is $\sigma^{*2} = k(x^*, x^*) - k(x^*, x_1)^2/(k(x_1, x_1) + \sigma_n^2)$. In the example, $1 - 0.368/1.1 = 0.666$. Two facts follow from the formula. The variance does not depend on the observed value $y_1$, only on where the data are, which is why GP-based active learning can plan where to sample before running anything. And with noise, the variance at an observed point does not fall to zero: at $x^* = x_1$ it is $1 - 1/1.1 = 0.09$, reflecting that a noisy run does not pin the function down exactly.

## Two observations

With observations $y$ at points $X$, the posterior mean is $\mu^* = m + k_*^\top (K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}(y - m)$, where $K$ is the kernel matrix of the data and $k_*$ the kernel between the query and each point. With zero mean, no noise, $y = (1, 2)$ at $x = 0$ and 1, and $x^* = 0.5$: $K$ has ones on the diagonal and $e^{-0.5} = 0.607$ off it, $\alpha = K^{-1}y = (-0.337, 2.204)$ and $k_* = (0.882, 0.882)$, so $\mu^* = 1.648$. Correlated data points share credit through $K^{-1}$. Each solve costs $O(n^3)$ in the number of runs, harmless for the tens to hundreds of runs an analog loop affords.

## Going deeper

Rasmussen and Williams, "Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning" (2006), chapter 2.

lesson:
# Acquisition functions: EI and UCB

Bayesian optimization chooses the next expensive run by maximizing an acquisition function computed from the GP posterior. Expected improvement and confidence bounds are the common choices. Each balances exploiting points with good predicted values against exploring points with high uncertainty, and the balance decides how many runs the search needs.

## Expected improvement

When minimizing, with best observed value $f^*$ and a Gaussian posterior with mean $\mu$ and standard deviation $\sigma$ at a candidate, the expected improvement is $\mathrm{EI} = (f^* - \mu)\Phi(z) + \sigma\varphi(z)$ with $z = (f^* - \mu)/\sigma$. For $f^* = 70$ mW, $\mu = 67$ mW and $\sigma = 5$ mW, $z = 0.6$, $\Phi(z) = 0.726$ and $\varphi(z) = 0.333$, so $\mathrm{EI} = 3 \cdot 0.726 + 5 \cdot 0.333 = 3.84$ mW. EI is the expectation of $\max(0, f^* - f)$, so it is never negative, and it is positive even where the mean is worse than $f^*$, as long as there is uncertainty.

## Confidence bounds

The lower confidence bound for minimization, $\mu - \kappa\sigma$, scores a candidate by an optimistic estimate of its value; the next run goes to the candidate with the smallest bound. With $\kappa = 1$, a candidate with mean 64 and standard deviation 4 has bound 60, and one with mean 75 and standard deviation 9 has bound 66, so the first wins. With $\kappa = 3$ the bounds are 52 and 48 and the uncertain one wins. $\kappa$ sets exploration explicitly. Maximization uses the upper bound $\mu + \kappa\sigma$ (UCB); confusing the two directions sends the search toward the worst candidates.

## Comparing candidates

EI trades mean against uncertainty automatically. With $f^* = 65$ uW, a candidate with mean 64 and standard deviation 3 has EI 1.76, one with mean 66 and standard deviation 4 has EI 1.15, and one with mean 61 and standard deviation 2 has EI 4.02. The third, with the best mean, wins here, but a candidate with a worse mean can win when its standard deviation is large enough. EI tends to exploit once the posterior is confident, so practical loops add exploration, run batches of candidates in parallel, and stop on a budget rather than when EI becomes small, since a miscalibrated GP can report small EI everywhere while missing the optimum.

## Going deeper

Frazier, "A Tutorial on Bayesian Optimization" (2018); Jones, Schonlau and Welch, "Efficient Global Optimization of Expensive Black-Box Functions," Journal of Global Optimization (1998).

label: Bayesian optimization for analog sizing
lesson:
# Bayesian optimization for analog sizing

Analog sizing chooses transistor widths, lengths, bias currents and capacitors to meet specifications such as gain, bandwidth and phase margin while minimizing power or area. Each evaluation is a SPICE run, often over corners. Bayesian optimization fits this setting because it needs few runs, but the constraints must be modeled as carefully as the objective.

## Modeling a constraint

A separate GP models each constrained quantity, such as phase margin. At a candidate sizing, if the phase-margin posterior is Gaussian with mean 63 degrees and standard deviation 4 degrees and the specification is at least 60 degrees, the probability of feasibility is $\Phi((63 - 60)/4) = \Phi(0.75) = 0.773$. The probability is low far from feasible data and near the boundary, and close to one deep inside the feasible region. Specifications checked at several process corners need the constraint at each corner, or a model of the worst corner, because a sizing feasible at the typical corner can fail at slow-slow.

## Constrained expected improvement

A standard way to fold constraints into the search multiplies expected improvement in the objective by the probability of feasibility, assuming the models are independent. If the best feasible power is 3.0 mW and a candidate's power posterior has mean 3.2 mW and standard deviation 0.4 mW, $z = -0.5$ and $\mathrm{EI} = -0.2 \cdot 0.309 + 0.4 \cdot 0.352 = 0.079$ mW. With feasibility probability 0.773, the constrained EI is 0.061 mW. A candidate that promises low power but is probably infeasible scores low, which keeps the search near the region the design can actually use.

## The feasible incumbent

The incumbent $f^*$ in constrained EI must be the best observed value among feasible runs. If runs gave 1.35 mW at phase margin 51 degrees and 3.94 mW at 57 degrees against a 55-degree specification, the incumbent is 3.94 mW, not 1.35. Using the infeasible value makes every feasible candidate look like no improvement, and the search stalls. If no run is yet feasible, the loop should first maximize the probability of feasibility. Sizing results from BO are still candidates: the final sizing needs full corner and Monte Carlo verification, and the layout parasitics change the numbers again.

## Going deeper

Gardner et al., "Bayesian Optimization with Inequality Constraints" (ICML 2014); Razavi, "Design of Analog CMOS Integrated Circuits" (2nd ed., 2017), for the specifications being optimized.

# Flow parameter tuning with multi-fidelity search

A physical-design flow has dozens of parameters: target density, timing-driven weights, routing layer limits, clock-tree options. Tuning them per design is a black-box search where each full run takes hours. Autotuners, such as the AutoTuner shipped with OpenROAD-flow-scripts, combine model-based search with early stopping of unpromising runs, which is where most of the saving comes from.

## Successive halving

Successive halving starts many configurations on a small budget and repeatedly keeps the best fraction $1/\eta$, giving each survivor $\eta$ times more budget. With 27 configurations, $\eta = 3$ and a first budget of 1 CPU-hour, 9 survive the first elimination, 3 the second and 1 the third. In a flow, budget can be stages reached (stop after placement, after clock-tree synthesis, after global route) or optimizer iterations. The method assumes that a configuration's early result ranks it roughly where its final result would. If that assumption fails, the method discards good configurations early and never sees them again.

## Counting the cost

Each rung costs the number of survivors times their budget. With 27 configurations, $\eta = 3$ and 1 hour: $27 \cdot 1 + 9 \cdot 3 + 3 \cdot 9 + 1 \cdot 27 = 108$ CPU-hours, if each rung restarts from scratch. Every rung costs the same 27 hours, so the total is the number of rungs times $n r$. Running all 27 configurations at the final budget of 27 hours would cost 729 hours, so the search is $729/108 = 6.75$ times cheaper. Warm-starting survivors from their previous checkpoint saves more, and Hyperband runs several such brackets with different starting budgets to hedge against a bad early ranking.

## When early results mislead

The saving is real only if short runs rank configurations as full runs would. In a flow, a configuration that looks good after placement can fail after routing, for example a high target density with low HPWL and later routing congestion. Low-fidelity metrics must therefore correlate with the final objective, and the correlation should be measured, for example by rank correlation between stage-level and final QoR over past runs. Multi-objective goals (timing, power and area together) need a Pareto front rather than one score, and a tuned configuration found for one design is a starting point for the next, not a guarantee.

## Going deeper

# Differentiable placement

Analytical global placement minimizes a smooth wirelength plus a density penalty over cell coordinates. DREAMPlace observed that this is the same computation as training a neural network: coordinates are the parameters, wirelength and density are the loss, and the gradients come from operators that a deep-learning toolkit runs on a GPU. The result is the same algorithm much faster, not a learned placer.

## Weighted-average wirelength

HPWL, the span of a net's pins, is not differentiable at the extreme pins and has zero gradient at interior pins. The weighted-average model replaces max and min by soft versions: $\mathrm{WA}_x = \frac{\sum x_i e^{x_i/\gamma}}{\sum e^{x_i/\gamma}} - \frac{\sum x_i e^{-x_i/\gamma}}{\sum e^{-x_i/\gamma}}$. For pins at $x = 0$, 4 and 10 um with $\gamma = 2$ um, the soft max is near 9.6 and the soft min near 0.5, and $\mathrm{WA}_x = 9.12$ um against an HPWL span of 10 um. Every pin now has a nonzero gradient, so the optimizer moves interior pins as well.

## The smoothing gap

WA underestimates the true span, and the gap shrinks with $\gamma$. For the same pins, $\gamma = 2$ gives a gap of 0.88 um and $\gamma = 1$ a gap of 0.09 um. A large $\gamma$ gives smooth, informative gradients early, when cells are far from their final places; a small one makes the objective match HPWL near the end. Placers therefore shrink $\gamma$ over the iterations, a continuation method that solves a sequence of easier problems on the way to the real one. The same idea appears in the log-sum-exp wirelength model, which overestimates instead.

## Placement as training

With loss $\mathrm{WL} + \lambda D$, where $D$ is an electrostatic density penalty, a step updates each cell by $x \leftarrow x - \eta(\partial \mathrm{WL}/\partial x + \lambda\, \partial D/\partial x)$. A cell at $x = 12$ um with gradients -1.4 and 1.9, $\lambda = 4$ and step 0.5 moves to $12 - 0.5(-1.4 + 7.6) = 8.9$ um. DREAMPlace implements wirelength and density as custom operators with hand-written backward kernels, uses Nesterov's method with adaptive steps, and raises $\lambda$ over iterations so that density increasingly dominates. The output is a global placement that still needs legalization and detailed placement.

# Smooth maximum for differentiable timing

Static timing takes a max at every gate input: the output arrives after the latest input. The max has a gradient only through the latest input, which stalls gradient-based optimization. Replacing it by the log-sum-exp soft maximum makes arrival times differentiable in every delay, at a controlled cost in accuracy. The temperature $\gamma$ sets the trade.

## Log-sum-exp

The soft maximum is $\mathrm{LSE}_\gamma(a) = \gamma \ln \sum_i e^{a_i/\gamma}$. Compute it stably by factoring out the largest value: $\mathrm{LSE}_\gamma(a) = a_{\max} + \gamma \ln \sum_i e^{(a_i - a_{\max})/\gamma}$, which avoids overflow for arrival times of hundreds of picoseconds. For arrivals 50 and 48 ps and $\gamma = 2$ ps, $\mathrm{LSE} = 50 + 2\ln(1 + e^{-1}) = 50.63$ ps. As $\gamma \to 0$ it approaches the max; as $\gamma$ grows it approaches a scaled sum. Inputs far below the max contribute almost nothing, so LSE behaves like max where one input clearly dominates.

## How much it overestimates

LSE always lies between the true max and the max plus $\gamma \ln n$ for $n$ inputs. In the example the gap is 0.63 ps, within the bound $2 \ln 2 = 1.39$ ps. The gap is largest when the inputs tie and vanishes when one dominates. Because LSE overestimates, a smoothed timer is pessimistic: it reports slightly later arrivals than STA, and the error accumulates along a path, one max per gate. A differentiable timer therefore uses a small $\gamma$, reports true STA numbers for evaluation, and uses the smooth values only for the gradients that steer optimization.

## Gradients through the soft max

The derivative of LSE with respect to input $i$ is the softmax weight $e^{a_i/\gamma}/\sum_j e^{a_j/\gamma}$. For arrivals 50 and 48 ps and $\gamma = 2$, the later input gets weight $1/(1 + e^{-1}) = 0.731$ and the other 0.269. The weights sum to one, so the gradient of an arrival is shared among inputs by how close they are to critical. With a hard max the latest input would get all of it and a near-critical input none, so an optimizer would fix one path and expose the next. The soft gradient lets it improve the near-critical paths together.

## Going deeper

Guo and Lin, "Differentiable-Timing-Driven Global Placement" (DAC 2022); Boyd and Vandenberghe, "Convex Optimization" (2004), section 3.1.5, on log-sum-exp.

# Differentiable static timing

A differentiable timer propagates smoothed arrival times through the timing graph so that a timing objective, such as total negative slack, has a gradient with respect to every delay and, through delay models, with respect to cell positions or sizes. It lets a gradient-based placer optimize timing directly instead of through net weights. The chain rule does the work, and the approximations decide whether it helps signoff.

## Smoothed arrival at a gate

At gate G with inputs arriving at $a_i$ through arcs of delay $d_i$, STA computes $A = \max_i (a_i + d_i)$. A differentiable timer computes $A = \mathrm{LSE}_\gamma(a_i + d_i)$. With arc sums 132 and 128 ps and $\gamma = 4$ ps, $A = 132 + 4\ln(1 + e^{-1}) = 133.25$ ps. Propagation runs in topological order exactly as in STA, so it costs one pass over the graph, and the same pass in reverse computes gradients. Arc delays themselves come from a differentiable delay model, for example Elmore delay on an estimated wire, which links $A$ to cell positions.

## The chain rule through a soft max

The derivative of $A$ with respect to an arc delay is the softmax weight of that input: $\partial A/\partial d_1 = e^{(a_1 + d_1)/\gamma}/\sum_j e^{(a_j + d_j)/\gamma}$. In the example it is 0.731. Gradients compose along paths: if an endpoint's arrival depends on $A$ with coefficient 1, it inherits the same 0.731. Backpropagation computes all such derivatives in one reverse pass, the same way a neural network's gradients are computed, which is why such timers are written as operators in a deep-learning toolkit and run on a GPU. The cost of the backward pass is the same order as the forward pass, linear in the size of the timing graph.

## Gradient of TNS

Total negative slack is $\mathrm{TNS} = \sum_j \max(0, -\mathrm{slack}_j)$, summed over endpoints. Each violating endpoint contributes the derivative of its arrival; each passing endpoint contributes zero. If G feeds two endpoints, one violating and one passing, then $\partial \mathrm{TNS}/\partial d_1 = 0.731$; if both violate, it is $2 \times 0.731 = 1.46$, since reducing $d_1$ helps both. The hinge is itself non-smooth at zero slack, so implementations smooth it too or accept a subgradient. The result guides placement; signoff STA on the routed design still measures whether timing improved. A WNS objective, by contrast, gives gradient only through the single worst endpoint unless it too is smoothed.

Guo and Lin, "Differentiable-Timing-Driven Global Placement" (DAC 2022); Lin et al., "DREAMPlace" (DAC 2019).
